entities.name: Francisco Pizarro
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Francisco Pizarro, a Spanish conquistador of humble origins, indelibly reshaped the geopolitical landscape of South America through his brutal yet strategically adept conquest of the vast Inca Empire. Born in Trujillo, Extremadura, likely in the 1470s, Pizarro's career epitomized the ambition and ruthlessness of early modern European expansion. His expeditions, commencing in the 1520s, culminated in the overthrow of one of the world's largest indigenous empires, introducing Spanish colonial rule and profoundly altering the demographic, cultural, and economic trajectories of the Andean region for centuries to come. His actions stand as a pivotal moment in the global expansion of European power, marking a violent collision of civilizations.

Pizarro's campaigns, driven by persistent rumors of immense wealth, began in earnest in 1531. With a meager force of fewer than 200 men, he exploited the internal strife between Inca half-brothers Atahualpa and Huáscar, a civil war that had severely weakened the empire. In November 1532, Pizarro orchestrated the infamous ambush at Cajamarca, capturing Emperor Atahualpa despite the Inca's overwhelming numerical superiority. Following the execution of Atahualpa in 1533, even after receiving an unprecedented ransom of gold and silver, Pizarro marched on the Inca capital of Cusco, completing its seizure later that year. This decisive victory, achieved through a combination of military technology, disease, and political manipulation, paved the way for the establishment of the Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru.
